title: The Econometrics of Financial Markets
research_question: Do quarterly earnings announcements convey information that affects the market valuation of firms' equity, and does the magnitude of any valuation effect depend on whether the announced earnings exceed, meet, or fall short of prior market expectations?
data_description: The illustrative sample consists of 600 quarterly earnings announcements for the thirty firms in the Dow Jones Industrial Index over the five-year period from January 1989 to December 1993, covering quarterly earnings from the last quarter of 1988 through the third quarter of 1993. For each firm-quarter, three items are compiled: the announcement date (from Datastream), actual announced earnings (from Compustat), and the mean analyst earnings forecast taken from the last month of the quarter (from I/B/E/S) as a proxy for market expectations. Daily stock returns are used as the unit of observation, along with the CRSP value-weighted index as the market portfolio. A 41-day window centered on the announcement (20 days before, the announcement day, and 20 days after) is examined, with the prior 250 trading days used to estimate normal-return parameters.
institutional_context: The Financial Accounting Standards Board and the Securities and Exchange Commission set reporting regulations intended to make financial statements informative about firm value, and quarterly earnings disclosures are a key recurring channel through which firms convey performance information to investors. Because rational markets should impound new information into prices quickly, quarterly earnings releases provide a well-defined, frequently occurring information event whose informational content can be assessed via short-horizon price reactions. Announcements are classified into three categories based on the deviation of actual earnings from the mean analyst forecast: 'good news' if actual earnings exceed expected by more than 2.5%, 'bad news' if they fall short by more than 2.5%, and 'no news' if they lie within a 5% band around expectations. Of the 600 announcements, 189 are classified as good news, 173 as no news, and 238 as bad news.
